provider: Zenodo anonymous download throughput (the fetch-serving question)

free_tier.stated: Each record has a default storage quota of 50 GB, with an unlimited number of records under 50 GB, plus an additional allowance of up to 150 GB to distribute across uploads; no period is stated.
free_tier.notes: The 50 GB quota applies per record; the 150 GB is one total allowance assigned to records from the storage settings. The per-record cap, the request rate and the retention window are in limits[].

per_object_cap.stated: No per-object cap documented in published terms; absence is not an unlimited claim.
per_object_cap.notes: extraction found no per-object clause; some of these providers meter on object count rather than bytes, and some state no cap

retention.stated: No retention statement documented in published terms; absence is not an unlimited claim.
retention.notes: extraction found no retention clause; the seed's limits text may still state one, see extras.limits_verbatim

egress.terms: Free and unmetered, and HTTP Range (206) is supported anonymously, which is what makes the parallel read possible: 'accept-ranges: bytes', 'content-range: bytes 0-1023/81165133690'.

tooling: zenodo_get (pip) already parallelises; any HTTP client with range support (aria2c -x/-s, rclone non-backend http, curl --parallel) will do.
chaining: Per-connection shaping limits transfers to approximately 350-480 KB/s, requiring client-side concurrency rather than account multiplication. Measured throughput scaling: 1 connection yields 0.3 MB/s, 6 connections yield 2.33 MB/s, 16 connections yield 6.01 MB/s, 32 connections yield 11.95 MB/s, and 64 connections yield 23.07 MB/s. At 23 MB/s aggregate bandwidth delivers approximately 2 TB per day from a single host.

limits.value: 50 GB per record default; 200 GB absolute ceiling on a single record with the 150 GB allowance pooled in; max 100 files per record (new API: 'a limit of 50GB total in the record (and any given file), and up to 100 files in the record').

limits_note: Bandwidth shaping is enforced per TCP connection rather than per IP address. Sixty-four concurrent HTTP Range requests all returned HTTP 206 and aggregate throughput saturated local network capacity without an aggregate cap.

identity_cost.detail: inferred from the category 'academic'; the source record states no identity cost, so this is a class assumption, not evidence

reliability_note: Single-stream downloads are painfully slow (~215 KB/s on a 100MB range; the same range took 120s to deliver 45MB). Anything that does not parallelise will appear broken. Reading one file sequentially is a ~50x underuse of the link.
confidence_note: The read path and served byte count were measured on 2026-10-30 against published repository objects. Documented with supporting probe data.

extras.verify_notes: All quota numbers confirmed unchanged. The dossier's throughput claim is directionally right and I reproduced it independently today: the throttle is PER CONNECTION, not per IP or per account. 1 conn 0.48 MB/s -> 8 conns 4.93 MB/s (10.3x for 8x) -> 32 conns 19.68 MB/s (4.0x for 4x, perfectly linear). 19.68 MB/s = ~1.70 TB/day, so one host meets the 1 TiB/day serving workload with ~1.7x headroom. Correction to the dossier's scaling table: my 32-conn number is 19.7 MB/s where the dossier recorded 11.95 MB/s — today's link is faster, the shape (linear, no knee) is identical. The 416s I saw were self-inflicted (my 32nd offset ran past the 7.77 GB EOF), not throttling. The new-API file cap: 100 files per record, which matters for sharding — 50 GB must be split into no more than 100 files, i.e. >=500 MB per file.

binding_note: the per-object cap sets the shard size and therefore the object count; it bounds the total more tightly than any headline quota
